transcript.content:
Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Reykjavik, Iceland at 2026-04-14 12:21 GMT (UTC+0000) (2026-04-14T12:21:00Z in UTC), at latitude 64.1466 degrees and longitude -21.9426 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 34.122 degrees and its azimuth is 159.921 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 18.176 degrees and its azimuth is 200.971 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 11.39 percent illuminated, 39.356 degrees from the Sun, and 375827.9 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To give you an honest estimate: **No, you will almost certainly not be able to see it.**

Here is the breakdown of why your intuition is correct, despite the app saying it is "above the horizon."

### 1. The "Daylight Washout" Factor
The biggest hurdle is the Sun. You mentioned the Sun is at an altitude of **34.1°**. At that height, the atmosphere is scattering a massive amount of sunlight. This creates a "veiling luminance" that drowns out almost everything in the sky except for the brightest objects (like Venus or Jupiter, and only then if they are high enough).

### 2. The Moon's Phase and Magnitude
You noted the Moon is only **11.39% illuminated**. This means it is a very thin waxing crescent. 
*   A Full Moon has a magnitude of about -12.6 (extremely bright).
*   A thin crescent moon, depending on its exact phase, usually has a magnitude between **-6 and -8**.
*   The Sun has a magnitude of **-26.7**.

Because the Moon is so poorly illuminated and the Sun is so high in the sky, the contrast ratio is simply too wide. The Moon will be "lost" in the glare of the blue sky.

### 3. The Geometry (The "Look" Test)
The Sun is at an azimuth of **~160°** (South-Southeast) and the Moon is at **~201°** (South-Southwest). 
*   This means the Moon is only about 40 degrees away from the Sun in the sky.
*   Because they are relatively close together, the Moon is sitting in the brightest part of the sky—the area of highest atmospheric scattering. 

### The "Maybe" Exception
The only way you would see it is if you were looking through a very high-quality pair of binoculars or a telescope. Even then, it would be difficult because the "background" of the sky would be so bright that the Moon wouldn't stand out clearly.

**Final Verdict:** You are right to be skeptical. Even though the app confirms it is physically above the horizon, the **photometric contrast** is too low. To your unaided eyes, the sky will just look like a bright, clear blue.
